newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan rebels say enter Kabul, take airport.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels say enter Kabul, take airport.

text.p: Afghanistan's rebel Taleban Islamic militia said they had entered parts of Kabul on Thursday and taken its airport as government troops appeared to be abandoning the besieged city.

The disused Khwaja Rawash airport in the northeast of the city was taken at night after the capture of the Soviet-built Microrayon housing complex in eastern Kabul, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service quoted a Taleban spokesman, Mullah Abdul Qadeer, as saying.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report, which also said the Taleban had taken Kohe Asmai hill, known as Television Hill, in the middle of Kabul.
But witnesses in Kabul said government troops appeared to be abandoning the capital as rebel Taleban forces were poised on the edge of the city.

A Reuters correspondent in Kabul, Alistair Lyon, said the city was "like a ghost town" with troops abandoning checkpoints and tanks and trucks laden with government soldiers had been seen heading north out of the city.
He reported there were few signs of fighting, with only sporadic exchanges of machine-gun and small arms fire heard from the edges of the city.

There was no sign that the Taleban forces were advancing into the city but there seemed little to stop them. They were earlier reported to have penetrated to within five km (three miles) of the presidential palace.
The security ministry building had been abandoned and was empty and at least six tanks and several trucks full of troops had been seen leaving the city.
The Taleban controls most of Afghanistan and seeks to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani to enforce a strict Islamic order in the country.
Earlier, a government spokesman told reporters in Kabul that government forces would fight to the death to defend the capital.
"We are establishing defences in every street of Kabul," said spokesman Amrullah as the two sides fought on in the city's outskirts, ignoring a U.N. Security Council call for an immediate ceasefire.
Government fighters guarding the main road east of Kabul said the rebels had seized the nearby military academy hours after a spokesman said it was in government hands.
Government troops were seen feverishly digging new positions in the Microrayon earlier in the evening while tanks also made defensive manoeuvres.
Witnesses in Kabul said fighting in the east appeared to have intensified as darkness fell with rockets landing in the city. But there was no word on casualties.
Government fighters said the Taleban were trying to advance on a new road to the government's main airbase at Bagram, north of Kabul. The old road to Bagram was in government hands.
A tank in the middle of the road fired at Taleban positions while small arms fire could also be heard in the north.
"We have thousands of volunteers from the city," said Amrullah, who speaks for Rabbani's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
"We are not short of ammunition, fuel, morale or motive. We will remain in Kabul whether we are on the earth or beneath it."
Amrullah said the Taleban had lost hundreds of men to reach the eastern outskirts of Pul-i-Charkhi "and will perhaps lose thousands in Kabul".

An official of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Jan-Luc Paladini, said there had been hundreds of dead and wounded on both sides in the past two days of fighting, but he had no details.
He said the ICRC had medical stocks in Kabul to last for six months and the ICRC relief department had been bringing more over the past few days.

The ICRC on Thursday stopped all flights from Bagram to the Pakistani city of Peshawar, fearing the military situation could worsen, after evacuating 50 people, including 16 ICRC delegates, leaving only staff needed for emergencies.
But Paladini said: "The ICRC is staying in Kabul. We are not leaving."
Taleban sources in Pakistan said the militia had further advanced from the south into the shattered city, taken Pul-i-Charkhi and the nearby military academy and Bagrami district in the southeast.
Amrullah accused Pakistan of sending military technicians to help the Taleban and said other countries, which he refused to name, were also aiding the rebels.
"We are defending the country's pride against Pakistani puppets. Pakistan wants to control our country. We are ready to give as much sacrifice as required. We don't mind if we die."
But Pakistan denied the accusations.
"We have had and will continue to observe total neutrality while we must maintain a close watch on the events as they develop," a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman said in Islamabad.
The 15-nation U.N. Security Council appealed for a ceasefire and peace talks after a meeting in New York on Wednesday.
Amrullah criticised the United Nations for what he said was inaction when Kabul was on the verge of a catastrophe.
"They know there could be a massacre in Kabul and massive violation of so-called human rights, but they are just watching," he said.
